# Plan: rate limiting for the orders API

One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

content.name: ask

questions.question: Should rate limiting apply only to POST /orders?

options.label: Yes — limit only POST /orders
options.tradeoff: Protects the expensive write path while leaving cheap GET reads unrestricted; smallest blast radius and easiest to reason about.
options.description: Only POST /orders consumes rate-limit budget.
options.holds_when: The abuse scenario is order-creation floods and GET /orders is not a concern.

options.label: No — also limit GET /orders, but with a separate higher limit
options.tradeoff: Defends against enumeration/burst on reads too, but adds a second bucket and more knobs to tune.
options.description: POST and GET each get their own bucket/key.

options.label: No — limit all routes with the same bucket
options.tradeoff: Simplest global rule, but a burst of GETs could starve POSTs for the same customer.
options.description: All requests from a customer share one limit.

brief.where: src/server.ts currently enforces x-customer-id then routes POST /orders (expensive DB write) and GET /orders (cheap list).
brief.what: Decide which routes are in scope before choosing keys, algorithms, or rollout.
brief.how: If you choose only POST /orders, the next round focuses on a single bucket and response path; if you include GET /orders, we'll need a second bucket/limit and precedence rules.

questions.question: Should the limit key be the x-customer-id header?

options.label: Yes — key on x-customer-id
options.tradeoff: Matches existing auth/identity header; isolates each customer so one misbehaving script cannot exhaust a shared IP pool.
options.description: Use req.headers.get('x-customer-id') as the rate-limit key.

options.label: No — key on client IP
options.tradeoff: Customers behind NAT/CDN share IPs, and the load balancer may not forward the real IP; enterprise scripts may rotate IPs.
options.description: Use the request's visible IP address as the key.

options.label: No — combine both x-customer-id and IP
options.tradeoff: More granular but means a single customer with multiple egress IPs gets multiple quotas, which can under- or over-limit.
options.description: Key is a composite of customer id and IP.

brief.where: src/server.ts:7 requires x-customer-id and returns 401 if missing; the load balancer is round-robin across three instances.
brief.what: Choose the dimension that identifies a 'customer' for quota accounting.
brief.how: This decides whether enterprise limits, rollout exemptions, and a future allowlist are keyed to customer id or IP.

questions.question: Should we use a token-bucket algorithm?

options.label: Yes — token bucket
options.tradeoff: Allows legitimate enterprise bursts while capping sustained rate; fits known scripted-burst behavior.
options.description: Bucket has capacity + refill rate; requests consume tokens.

options.label: No — fixed window
options.tradeoff: Cheapest Redis operation, but a burst can double-spike at window boundaries and you need a clock-alignment story.
options.description: Count requests in fixed time windows.

options.label: No — sliding window log
options.tradeoff: Most precise boundary behavior, but more Redis memory/CPU per key.
options.description: Store timestamps of each request and expire old ones.

brief.where: PLAN.md notes ~20 enterprise customers legitimately burst, and the incident was 40,000 orders in 10 minutes.
brief.what: Choose the counting algorithm that shapes the traffic.
brief.how: The algorithm constrains refill/burst parameters, Redis Lua script choice, and how aggressive the rollout can be.

questions.question: Should counters live in the existing Redis 7 cluster?

options.label: Yes — shared Redis cluster
options.tradeoff: Correct global quota across all three instances; reuses existing cluster but adds a dependency.
options.description: Use Redis for token/ window counters.

options.label: No — instance memory
options.tradeoff: No external dependency and sub-millisecond, but round-robin means a customer effectively gets 3× the intended quota and limits reset per deploy.
options.description: Store counters in-process (e.g., Map) on each server instance.

brief.where: PLAN.md says three instances behind round-robin LB and Redis 7 is already used for sessions by another service.
brief.how: This determines whether quotas are global, how failover behaves, and whether Redis unavailability can break order creation.

questions.question: Should enterprise customers get higher per-customer limits stored in config owned by customer success?

options.label: Yes — per-customer limits in config/DB, owned by customer success
options.tradeoff: Prevents engineering from being a bottleneck for limit changes; requires a small config table/schema.
options.description: Map x-customer-id → bucket capacity/refill; customer success/account-ops owns values.

options.label: No — same limit for everyone, no special path
options.tradeoff: No extra data model, but legitimate enterprise bursts may be throttled unless the default limit is very high.
options.description: Default token-bucket parameters apply to all customer ids.

options.label: No — hard-coded engineering allowlist instead
options.tradeoff: Fast to ship but creates ongoing code-change churn and deploy coupling.
options.description: A static list of enterprise customer ids with elevated limits in source code.

brief.where: PLAN.md lists ~20 enterprise customers with scripted integrations and asks how they get higher limits and who owns the numbers.
brief.what: Decide the enterprise exemption mechanism and owner.
brief.how: This unblocks the rollout: we need to know whether existing enterprise customers get pre-negotiated quotas before enforcement begins.

questions.question: Should rejected clients receive HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header?

options.label: Yes — 429 with Retry-After
options.tradeoff: Standard, cache-friendly signal that automated clients can back off from; requires computing remaining-window/retry time.
options.description: Return 429 and include Retry-After (seconds or datetime).

options.label: No — 429 without Retry-After
options.tradeoff: Clients must guess backoff; simpler implementation but worse integration experience.
options.description: Return 429 only.

options.label: No — 503 Service Unavailable
options.tradeoff: Misleading status; Retry-After is allowed but 503 implies server-side outage rather than quota.
options.description: Return 503 with or without Retry-After.

brief.where: PLAN.md asks what a rejected client sees.
brief.what: Choose the HTTP status and headers returned when a customer exceeds their quota.
brief.how: This affects client retry logic, monitoring/alerting rules, and how support documents the behavior.

questions.question: Should rate limiting apply only to POST /orders?

options.label: Yes — limit only POST /orders
options.tradeoff: Protects the expensive write path while leaving cheap GET reads unrestricted; smallest blast radius and easiest to reason about.
options.description: Only POST /orders consumes rate-limit budget.
options.holds_when: The abuse scenario is order-creation floods and GET /orders is not a concern.

options.label: No — also limit GET /orders, but with a separate higher limit
options.tradeoff: Defends against enumeration/burst on reads too, but adds a second bucket and more knobs to tune.
options.description: POST and GET each get their own bucket/key.

options.label: No — limit all routes with the same bucket
options.tradeoff: Simplest global rule, but a burst of GETs could starve POSTs for the same customer.
options.description: All requests from a customer share one limit.

brief.where: src/server.ts currently enforces x-customer-id then routes POST /orders (expensive DB write) and GET /orders (cheap list).
brief.what: Decide which routes are in scope before choosing keys, algorithms, or rollout.
brief.how: If you choose only POST /orders, the next round focuses on a single bucket and response path; if you include GET /orders, we'll need a second bucket/limit and precedence rules.

questions.question: Should the limit key be the x-customer-id header?

options.label: Yes — key on x-customer-id
options.tradeoff: Matches existing auth/identity header; isolates each customer so one misbehaving script cannot exhaust a shared IP pool.
options.description: Use req.headers.get('x-customer-id') as the rate-limit key.

options.label: No — key on client IP
options.tradeoff: Customers behind NAT/CDN share IPs, and the load balancer may not forward the real IP; enterprise scripts may rotate IPs.
options.description: Use the request's visible IP address as the key.

options.label: No — combine both x-customer-id and IP
options.tradeoff: More granular but means a single customer with multiple egress IPs gets multiple quotas, which can under- or over-limit.
options.description: Key is a composite of customer id and IP.

brief.where: src/server.ts:7 requires x-customer-id and returns 401 if missing; the load balancer is round-robin across three instances.
brief.what: Choose the dimension that identifies a 'customer' for quota accounting.
brief.how: This decides whether enterprise limits, rollout exemptions, and a future allowlist are keyed to customer id or IP.

questions.question: Should we use a token-bucket algorithm?

options.label: Yes — token bucket
options.tradeoff: Allows legitimate enterprise bursts while capping sustained rate; fits known scripted-burst behavior.
options.description: Bucket has capacity + refill rate; requests consume tokens.

options.label: No — fixed window
options.tradeoff: Cheapest Redis operation, but a burst can double-spike at window boundaries and you need a clock-alignment story.
options.description: Count requests in fixed time windows.

options.label: No — sliding window log
options.tradeoff: Most precise boundary behavior, but more Redis memory/CPU per key.
options.description: Store timestamps of each request and expire old ones.

brief.where: PLAN.md notes ~20 enterprise customers legitimately burst, and the incident was 40,000 orders in 10 minutes.
brief.what: Choose the counting algorithm that shapes the traffic.
brief.how: The algorithm constrains refill/burst parameters, Redis Lua script choice, and how aggressive the rollout can be.

questions.question: Should counters live in the existing Redis 7 cluster?

options.label: Yes — shared Redis cluster
options.tradeoff: Correct global quota across all three instances; reuses existing cluster but adds a dependency.
options.description: Use Redis for token/ window counters.

options.label: No — instance memory
options.tradeoff: No external dependency and sub-millisecond, but round-robin means a customer effectively gets 3× the intended quota and limits reset per deploy.
options.description: Store counters in-process (e.g., Map) on each server instance.

brief.where: PLAN.md says three instances behind round-robin LB and Redis 7 is already used for sessions by another service.
brief.how: This determines whether quotas are global, how failover behaves, and whether Redis unavailability can break order creation.

questions.question: Should enterprise customers get higher per-customer limits stored in config owned by customer success?

options.label: Yes — per-customer limits in config/DB, owned by customer success
options.tradeoff: Prevents engineering from being a bottleneck for limit changes; requires a small config table/schema.
options.description: Map x-customer-id → bucket capacity/refill; customer success/account-ops owns values.

options.label: No — same limit for everyone, no special path
options.tradeoff: No extra data model, but legitimate enterprise bursts may be throttled unless the default limit is very high.
options.description: Default token-bucket parameters apply to all customer ids.

options.label: No — hard-coded engineering allowlist instead
options.tradeoff: Fast to ship but creates ongoing code-change churn and deploy coupling.
options.description: A static list of enterprise customer ids with elevated limits in source code.

brief.where: PLAN.md lists ~20 enterprise customers with scripted integrations and asks how they get higher limits and who owns the numbers.
brief.what: Decide the enterprise exemption mechanism and owner.
brief.how: This unblocks the rollout: we need to know whether existing enterprise customers get pre-negotiated quotas before enforcement begins.

questions.question: Should rejected clients receive HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header?

options.label: Yes — 429 with Retry-After
options.tradeoff: Standard, cache-friendly signal that automated clients can back off from; requires computing remaining-window/retry time.
options.description: Return 429 and include Retry-After (seconds or datetime).

options.label: No — 429 without Retry-After
options.tradeoff: Clients must guess backoff; simpler implementation but worse integration experience.
options.description: Return 429 only.

options.label: No — 503 Service Unavailable
options.tradeoff: Misleading status; Retry-After is allowed but 503 implies server-side outage rather than quota.
options.description: Return 503 with or without Retry-After.

brief.where: PLAN.md asks what a rejected client sees.
brief.what: Choose the HTTP status and headers returned when a customer exceeds their quota.
brief.how: This affects client retry logic, monitoring/alerting rules, and how support documents the behavior.
